basis: The sermon takes its text as the day's reading ('lectio hodierna monstravit') and opens on 'Ascendit, inquit, in naviculam, et transfretavit, et venit in civitatem suam', which the printing cites '(Matth. IX, 1)' in col. 339 (leaf n171). It expounds that verse spiritually and then says 'nunc ipsius historiae ordinem prosequamur' and walks the pericope in order: the paralytic offered on his bed and 'Confide, fili: dimittuntur tibi peccata tua' (9:2) and 'Hic blasphemat' (9:3) in col. 341, then 'Et cum vidisset, inquit, Jesus cogitationes eorum' through 'et surrexit et abiit in domum suam' (9:4-7) in col. 342 (leaf n172). It closes on 'Tolle lectum tuum' and 'Vade in domum tuam', and Sermo 51 follows. The crowds' fear and their glorifying of God in 9:8 are nowhere quoted or expounded, so the extent stops at 9:7, although the Gospel the 1962 calendar reads on the Eighteenth Sunday after Pentecost runs to 9:8. The Pharisees' 'quis enim potest peccata remittere nisi solus Deus?' is not Matthew's wording; Mark 2:7 and Luke 5:21 carry the question, and the sermon uses it inside its argument without expounding either Gospel. Read on the page images; the text layer is not collated.
date_basis: Not a composition date. This is the second case the header admits, in the form `composed_year` in scripts/_catena.py describes: work.peter-chrysologus.sermones carries `composed` as 'saec. V', because no closer dating of the collection or of this sermon is established, and a century gives the chain no year to order by, so the fragment must say what dates it. 450 is the year Migne's Patrologia Latina 52 prints for Chrysologus over its volume title page and Elenchus ('SAECULUM V. ANNUS 450.', leaves n8 and n9), which the work record's composed_basis quotes, and the year of his death in the Catholic Encyclopedia as src/sources/inventories/author-standing-v1.toml cites it. If the sermon is his, it was preached by then. That ascription is disputed, and this date rests on it (Rule 7): Patrologia Latina 57 prints the same text as Maximus of Turin's Homilia CVIII, and its editor reports manuscripts naming John Chrysostom, Severian and Maximus while declining to impugn the received ascription to Chrysologus. The evidence stands on this passage record and on passage.maximus-of-turin.homiliae.1862-migne-pl-57.homilia-108. Nothing here settles it.
